title: Reservoir Routing and Regional Throttle Strategy
content:
Summary

This note captures a pattern we are experimenting with for predictable, low-latency inference across multi-region clusters under capacity pressure. We call it the \"reservoir routing\" pattern: treat each region as a set of layered capacity reservoirs (reserved, elastic, overflow) with throttle \"valves\" in the control plane that open/close along deterministic policies. The goal is to provide: 1) clear priority semantics for customer classes and request types, 2) graceful utility-preserving degradations (reduced model size or quality modes, increased batching) rather than hard failures, and 3) safe regional spillover that respects latency SLOs and data-residency constraints.

High-level concepts and metaphors
- Reservoirs: capacity pools grouped by intent. Examples: \"reserved\" (dedicated instances for enterprise customers), \"elastic\" (autoscaling GPU pools), \"overflow\" (cheaper CPU/quantized endpoints or partner-hosted fallbacks). Think of them as tanks with different water quality and cost.
- Valves (throttle policies): control-plane knobs that allow flow from one reservoir to another, subject to policy guardrails (SLOs, cost budgets, compliance). Valves can be partial (allow X qps) or fully open/closed.
- Spillways (regional spillover): controlled routing from a saturated region to another region's reservoirs; usually constrained by latency budget and data-residency rules.

Routing primitives and decision surface
We want a small set of deterministic primitives the control plane speaks so routing is auditable and testable:
- region_priority_list: ordered list of regions by preference for a request (ex: [us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1]).
- capacity_class: one of [reserved, elastic, overflow].
- degrade_mode: one of [none, quantize, smaller-model, batched-latency-window, reduced-beams].
- max_latency_budget_ms: a user-visible SLO for the route.
- data_residency: {required_region: list} as freeform text (we surface as tags).
- cost_budget_usd_per_hour: soft budget to guide routing to cheaper reservoirs when open.

Policy examples (expressed as control-plane rules, pseudo language)
- Enterprise-reserved-first: if request.customer_tier == enterprise then prefer reservoirs.reserved in region_priority_list, fallback to elastic in same region only if latency_budget permits; never spill to non-compliant regions.
- Best-effort-spill: for public-tier requests, if primary_region.elastic_utilization > 0.85 then enable spillway to next_region.elastic until local_util drops below 0.7. Cap spill qps at 15% of receiving_region.elastic_capacity.
- Degrade-before-drop: if route.latency_estimate > max_latency_budget_ms and no elastic capacity available, attempt degrade_mode sequence [batched-latency-window -> quantize -> smaller-model] with cost/quality telemetry gating each step.

Model variant strategy
We maintain explicit families per logical model name with three recommended variants:
- full-fp16 (production-quality, highest cost)
- quantized-hybrid (FP16->4bit runs, lower cost, may introduce subtle output drift for sensitive tasks)
- cpu-fallback (CPU-optimized model for low QPS or emergency fallback)

Mapping rules:
- Each route has a model_fallback_chain: e.g. [full-fp16, quantized-hybrid, cpu-fallback]. The control plane attempts steps in order but may skip to a cheaper variant earlier if cost_budget triggers or observed quality regressions detected by eval hooks.
- Variant-selection heuristics include request type (embedding vs. generation), token_length_estimate, and customer_tier. For short completions we prefer quantized variants sooner; for safety-sensitive outputs we lock to full-fp16.

Tiered capacity plumbing and bookkeeping
- Capacity metadata: each instance exposes capacity tokens (tokens/sec and concurrent-requests) and quality tags (which variant). Central capacity index keeps per-region rollup with 1s resolution and 1min sliding windows for smoothing.
- Reservation accounting: reserved pools deduct immediately when a customer pins capacity. Elastic pools are soft; autoscaler grows/shrinks but we keep a floor to minimize cold starts.
- Overflow sinks: these are special endpoints with high concurrency but high latency (e.g., CPU boxes) that are only used as final fallback. They are billed differently and flagged in cost reports.

Regional spillover mechanics and safeguards
When a region crosses a saturation threshold we follow a three-step spill algorithm:
1) Local rebalancing: push requests to lower-priority reservoirs in same region (reserved -> elastic -> overflow) and toggle degrade_mode candidates.
2) Hemispheric spill: if local cannot satisfy, spill to sibling regions within the same hemisphere (e.g., us-west <-> us-east) respecting latency budget and data_residency. Prioritize regions with free elastic headroom.
3) Global emergency: if hemisphere cannot absorb, optionally open cross-hemisphere spillways for best-effort public-tier traffic only; enterprise requests remain local or per contract.

Safeguards:
- Latency gate: the control plane includes an estimate of RTT+processing; if estimated end-to-end > max_latency_budget_ms then we do NOT spill despite capacity shortage (instead switch to degrade_mode).
- Compliance gate: any request marked with data_residency constraints cannot be routed outside approved regions.
- Cost gate: a per-customer cost burn rate prevents uncontrolled spill that would create large cost surprises; spills increment a counter and alert at thresholds.

Control plane design and operational hooks
- Declarative policies: rules expressed as JSON/YAML in a policy store (we already have prototypes in github PR 812). Policies are versioned and rollout happens via canary toggles.
- Runtime decision service: a stateless router queries a central decision service with request metadata and capacity snapshot; decision service returns {target_region, reservoir, model_variant, degrade_mode, route_id}. The service is horizontally scalable and caches decisions for identical request keys for short durations.
- Observability: every decision emits a single line event with inputs + outputs + reasoning_code to tracing. Reasoning_code is a short tag identifying which rule fired (ex: \"spill_hemi_01\").

Testing and simulation plan
- Synthetic traffic playground: create reproducible traces that exercise different load shapes: steady spike, bursty tail, region outage, slowdowns (increased p99 latency). Run through simulator to verify valves and costs.
- Chaos scenarios: kill primary region control plane components and verify failover paths engage and that enterprise reservations remain honored.
- QA evals: for any new model_variant rollout, run evals on known failure-cases to estimate drift and quality loss under quantized or smaller-model modes. Gate automatic fallback for families that fail critical evals.

Runbook snippets (for on-call)
- Symptom: us-west-2 high rejection rate for public routes
  Action: check elastic_utilization > 90%? If yes, enable spillway to us-east-1 (open valve to 10% of us-east elastic capacity) and enable \"degrade-before-drop\" for public routes. Notify cost alert channel.
- Symptom: increased cross-region latency after spill enabled
  Action: revert spillway open percentage by 50%, disable cross-hemisphere spills, and switch high-latency requests to cpu-fallback with batched-latency-window if within cost tolerance.

Observability and post-mortems
- Key metrics: per-region reservoir utilization, spill_qps, degrade_mode_rate, variant_switch_rate, end-to-end p50/p95/p99, and per-customer cost burn.
- Post incident: always include a \"what degraded and why\" section that ties rule reasoning_code values to timeline events and links to simulator inputs that reproduce the scenario.

Open questions / trade-offs
- How aggressively should we batch when in degrade_mode? More batching saves cost but increases tail latency unpredictably. Proposal: configurable per-route max_batch_delay_ms with hard cap 200ms for interactive routes.
- When to allow cross-hemisphere spill for enterprise customers? We need a product knob in the console plus legal approvals.
- How to surface quality regressions automatically after a model_variant switch? We currently have eval harnesses but realtime signal detection for semantic drift is an area to mature.

Next steps and short-term deliverables (30–60 days)
- Implement valve open/close feature in policy engine and run canary for public-tier traffic. (owner: Daniel)
- Instrument reasoning_code and add to tracing pipeline (owner: Marta)
- Expand simulator to include hemisphere-level topology and cost modeling (owner: Olu)
- Draft console UI for per-route spill controls and visibility (owner: Priya)

Notes to reviewers
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic and focused on operational mechanics. I want feedback on the policy language and whether the reservoir metaphors help or confuse. Also please flag any contract/legal constraints around cross-region routing for enterprise customers I might have missed.

End of note.
